p:
We will have to get that information from our colleagues at MOIA as we uh wouldn’t have those specific details as to what they’re planning but we will follow up with you.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great, also in terms of uh, in terms of the Office of Asylum Seeker operations, it looks like the Preliminary Plan includes a reduction of $880,000 in state funding and eight positions in Fiscal ‘26, only we were curious about how that funding amount was determined and whether OWASSO has been officially disbanded.

Yes, uhm, so uh, the OWASSO staff and uhm, funding have been absorbed by uh, the very city agencies, primarily by DSS. Uhm, the state funding in the budget was just the - the modified budget that was in there. I have to get back to you on what that funding represented but uhm, yeah, I’d say OWASSO- OWASSO is - COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Is no more?
Yeah, yeah. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay, long overdue. So, the eight, the eight positions are now part of the DSS general budget have been reallocated?

Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay great, thank you. Uhm, and then lastly, just to follow up on uh Council Member Nurses questions about uh the shelter, ICE enforcement. Uhm, in particular, we are aware that

uhm, many of the security services that are in shelter are contracted services. Obviously they also are under the obligation of meeting our laws. We’ve talked a lot about it in the past. Uhm, but can you tell us uh again for the record, uhm, how uh security contractors are informed and held to account on maintaining uhm responsibilities for our laws?

Thank you Council Member. Uhm, as we mentioned earlier in response to Council Member Nurses question, these trainings, the communications, our contracted security providers, or the providers contracted securities were invited and did participate. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And in terms of the two instances where uhm, ICE was able to enter a facility without permission, uhm, what measures have you taken to ensure that contractors will never have this problem? They will never experience this failure again.

Yeah, again, thank you for the question. I think as we mentioned just constantly reiterating the process. Speaking with the teams after the incident. Also, to debrief to understand what kind of happened, so that we can talk

through next time. Uhm, but it is an ongoing effort to make sure that everybody understands the way to handle this, especially in the emergency situation. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Great and Chair, if I may just one more question?

I’ll give you two more. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Oh, she’s so kind. So many questions, so little time. And of course, I can’t find it now that I’m under the pressure of performance. Uhm, I’d like to move back to Homebase. Uhm, let me - okay here we go. Uhm, could you tell us uhm so, we know that HRA’s Homebase supports City FHEPS in community clients to maintain stable housing. Uhm, we know it’s a network of community based organizations that provide these homelessness prevention services. What’s the current Fiscal ‘26 budget for Homebase uhm, and is that amount baselined?

Uhm, the current budget for Homebase is $67.9 million. There is baselined funding in the budget that does fluctuate a bit to $66.6 in ‘26 going to $63.9 million in ‘27 and ‘28. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So, 90 percentage amount are baselined for that funding?
Yeah, largely baselined yeah. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Uhm, in terms of uhm what’s the actual spending to date in Fiscal ‘26? And how much was oh- uh yeah what was the actual for Fiscal ‘25?

Uhm, so through Fiscal - uhm through February for Fiscal Year ‘26, we’ve spent $46.5 million. The actuals for ‘25 were $67.9 million. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay and then in terms of uhm, in multiple City FHEPS oversight hearings, we had heard from the public that the demand for the City FHEPS application renewals and other rental assistance services that Homebase provides can’t be met with the current level of funding budgeted. We’ve also heard that CBO’s are having difficulty hiring and maintaining adequate staff levels. Uhm, as the PMMR notes, in the first four months of 2026, the program had over 12,000 enrollments, which is 14.2 percent increase compared to the same period of year. How many contracted providers are within the Homebase program?

Sure, there are 7 providers with 16 contracts and I believe it is 23 locations but I

will confirm that last uh piece for you. Uhm, we are aware that for some Homebase providers right, uh, uh, there are wait times to be seen. I will say every Homebase provider does an initial triage for everyone who reaches out to determine if there is an emergency need, such an imminent eviction or other, other activity that needs to be addressed and those individuals will be seen either that day or within you know the next day or two but we are - as I mentioned before, looking at ways in which we can uh, shift some of the responsibilities that have been taken on by Homebase over the years back into HRA so that we can expand capacity for them to uh serve more people in the community. That includes you know looking at things that we’re doing around subsidy work that they currently work on and especially around State FHEPS as well as some other complex case work that they do that we think we are able to bring back into the agency uh to expand their capacity. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So, since we’ve acknowledged there is a capacity issue, uhm, do you know what the current case ratio would be for Homebase staff at this moment?

Uhm, it doesn’t work on a case ratio basis in that manner. I will say you know uhm, uhm, last year, they did exceed their service targets, right, which was 30,000 served and they did serve uh, uh, 32,000 last year. So, it is something that we’re tracking closely and we’re in conversation, ongoing conversation with the Office of Management and Budget around resources for the program. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And, and, what’s the funding that you anticipate given what we know to date? The program Uhm, the program would need to operate optimally?

So, that is something we’re still discussing with OMB to identify what additional resources would be appropriate to help you know respond to the community need. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And lastly, so what is the directive when uhm - so it sounds like the Homebase providers are asked to prioritize and triage emergencies. How, how, is the agency uhm conducting oversight and evaluation that those triages are actually happening and happening promptly.

So, we uh, speak quite frequently with our Homebase providers uhm, uh, to assess what is happening. We talk to them about uh, where they may be seeing wait times. Uhm, and how that is manifesting itself within their work uhm and I will also say that they are uh - they definitely come forward to us when they are finding that there may be some challenges, especially if it’s relating to uh serving those who are showing up with an emergence need that needs to be addressed immediately. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay, thank you Chair. I’ll be back.

You’re welcome. I think that was about 4 questions that you actually asked. Uhm, but important ones, so thank you. Okay, I’m going to ask a couple questions on behalf of Council Member Thomas-Henry who is on Zoom. What is the process for someone in a shelter to apply for formerly homeless set asides in new housing developments? From her experience, shelter residents are applying directly through Housing Connect and the Housing Coordinators at some of the shelters do not seem to be well informed on the application process for the set asides or availability of new sites.

Uhm, I will take part of that and then we might get back to you and the Council Member with some additional details and I’ll ask my DH colleagues to weigh in as well. Uhm, so for HPD homeless set asides, right? Uh, the provider network is aware of the different availabilities that we have. Uhm, to apply for an HPD unit, you do have to submit through HPD Connect. I know that we do have data shares that we are doing with HPD to sort of share information on those individuals who have applied and are eligible but we’ll have to get back to you with some more specific details to map it out but obviously, we do want to know if our shelter providers right, if we’re hearing that some staff aren’t fully aware of the process in which it happened, that is something that we will uh discuss about and make sure that we’re pushing out information that’s clear and simple so that folks will ensure our individuals who could maybe you know benefit from those set asides, know that they’re available to them.
Great.

Yeah, thank you Administrator and I will add that uhm, it is uhm, first and foremost part

of the rehousing strategy for clients in shelter to have HHA submitted, so it is the job of shelter staff to ensure that that’s done, that it’s done accurately and when changes occur that things like income are updated.

We can connect Council Member Thomas-Henry with you all uhm to see if there’s a specific location that might need some more assistance. Thank you and then second question from her. Last year, a former JFK Hilton Hotel in Queens was converted to over 300 affordable apartments for low income and formerly homeless New Yorkers. As someone who represents a district with an airport that is surrounded by hotels that have been converted to shelters, is there a long term plan to replicate this model of converting hotels into permanent housing?

Uh, certainly so yes, so that conversion uh was part of the affordable housing services program that we have, uhm which you know we are definitely very supportive of and looking to expand if possible. I do know that there is sort of an overall interest as well across the Administration

to look at how other hotels could be transitioned to more affordable housing.
Great, thank you. I’m going to kick it over to Council Member Brewer before I continue on with my line of questioning.

Thank you. West 74th Street would be great permanent housing, I’m just saying because I am - you know the issues there Scott, oh my God. Alright, uhm, one question, how many city run shelters are there compared to run by nonprofits?
Thank you Council Member. THere are five city run shelters. When we exclude two intake facilities, Path and 30th Street.
Okay and are they going to be continuing? Are you going to have more or you’re probably going to stick with the nonprofit?
I think all plans are in discussion for those sites.

Okay. Next is uhm, I get a lot of calls about APS, Adult Protective Services. According to the uhm, Preliminary Management Plan, there’s an increase with like in the specifics as I think many of us are getting older, probably why but

there are many more requests and that’s an increase in cases. So, what is driving these increases except maybe age? How have you been able to handle the caseload, the referral volume, uhm and how many are denied? I must admit I get a lot- hoarders, which is a big problem. So, tons and tons of hoarders, APS, etc., and I think this is going to be a growing problem, a growing challenge. So, you obviously need case workers, you need a budget, uh home attendants. So, I’m just wanting to know how and generally, how you’re going to be addressing either budgetwise, staffing-wise, uhm, the issue of case workers and APS and the hoarding issue, which is prevalent.

Hmm, absolutely, thank you for the question. Uhm, so uhm I can say in regards to case workers over the last couple of years, we’ve hired an additional 107 case workers. We obviously track very closely uhm caseload ratios, uhm, the budget as well. You know I will say we are within our time limit rates to be assessing cases that are referred to us. I will also note that eligibility for APS is very clearly defined by the state and other regulations uhm and it’s sort of very specific criteria that needs to be met for someone to be identified as an

APS client, which includes sort of a combination of things of an individual. Needs to be 18 years or older uhm and they need to be mentally or physically impaired. They have to be unable to manage their resources, carry out the activities of daily living, or protect themselves from abuse, neglect, exploitation or other hazardous situations and have no one available who is willing or able to assist them responsibly. And so, we - all of those criteria need to be met to be deemed eligible for APS, otherwise the case would be declined at that moment. Uhm, but it is something that we’re tracking very, very closely. Uhm, I agree with you with you know the aging of the population as well. We want to make sure that we’re supporting individuals and we will assess and discuss with OMB as well where we see additional resources.
Do you have a contract for hoarding to clean out or do you do that internally because I do a lot of it myself.
We have a deep cleaning contract that we utilize when uh, uh, a hoarding situation has been encountered and we realize that some type of deep cleaning is necessary.
Could you let us know how much that is? How much it’s increased and if you think it needs to be more increased? Because it’s -
Yeah, we will follow up with you on that.
Thank you. Thank you Madam Chair.

Thank you Council Member. Okay, addressing chronic under budgeting in City FHEPS and cash assistance. In recent years, financial plans have not appropriately accounted for costs of HRA’s City FHEPS and cash assistance budget at a level proportionate with recent expenditures. THe chronic underbudgeting of these vital programs has been of concern to the Council and was raised in every Preliminary Budget responses since Fiscal 2019. The Council was pleased to see that the Preliminary Plan fills a fiscal cliff for City FHEPS and cash assistance. Increasing the baseline budget for both programs starting in Fiscal 2027. The funding added in the Preliminary Plan for City FHEPS brings the total Fiscal 2026 budget to $1.78 billion growing to $3.04 billion by Fiscal

2029. How do HRA and OMB forecast the growth of the City FHEPS program?

Yes, thank you for that question. So, as I noted earlier, uhm, I think in relation to shelters, we work very closely with the Office of Management and Budget. We work very closely with the Office of Management and Budget. We share data with them. Uhm, and we uh, you know work on Fiscal forecasts for this and other programs and reconcile those but based on what we’re seeing in the program themselves, in cases of rental assistance, the growth we’re seeing, uhm, the anticipated growth for the rental assistance vouchers and so forth.
Okay, can you provide a breakdown of the primary factors that drive the cost increases across the plan period.

Sure, yeah, I mean the increase there is again, new entrances into the program, which I noted earlier was about $15,000 for FY25. Uhm, we project with the voucher increases would be again, we - we follow the New York City Housing Authority and their payment standards. Those payment standards are set by HUD. Uhm, so we project the growth and payment standards uhm and overall, you know when you

look at the new entrances, the people that are leaving and the rental assistance, that’s how we project and what we think the populations would be.
How much has been spent to date in Fiscal 2026 on City FHEPS?
Give me one second. Uhm, so our spending through January was $1.1 billion.
Wait, through January?
Through January.
So, that would be- okay, $1.?
$1.1 billion.
Okay and then how much was spent in Fiscal ‘25?
Uhm, Fiscal ‘25, we spent uhm just under $1.4 billion.
Okay and how much of that went towards client benefits?
Uhm, that full amount was for just rental assistance. So, everything.
Okay.
That’s rental assistance, City FHEPS.
Okay. Hold on. We’ve seen consistent and significant growth in spending and enrollment in the program each year since inception. When does HRA believe the program may plateau?

So, I’ll just, I’ll jump in. I mean, just looking at the program which you know with the two weeks I’ve had on the ground. Uhm, there’s a lot of need and desire to use this program clearly and it’s helping people. If we keep of course letting people into the program and that’s good and they’re moving in and out of the shelter or avoiding shelter in the first place, uhm, but if there’s no exit to that program, it continues to grow, essentially endlessly. There’s really two degrees of freedom right? There’s ins and outs and if ins are always going to exceed outs and they are, without any other strategies, then it will continue to grow. There’s only so much of course that could be done in the middle, we should do our best job to run an efficient program to make sure that we meet rent standards but with increasing people entering the program uh and very few exits, it continues to grow.

Understood. As of the Preliminary Plan, cash assistance makes up 19.4

percent of HRA’s Fiscal 2026 budget at $2.76 billion and is baselined at 2.74 billion starting in Fiscal 2027. More households are enrolled in and staying on cash assistance for longer periods of time. According to the PMMR, the number of people receiving cash assistance that was - the number of people receiving cash assistance was 604,000 for the first four months of Fiscal 2026, which shows an increase from that period last year. How do HRA and OMB forecast growth for cash assistance?

Cash assistance again, you know we work pretty closely with OMB to project the uhm, the population for cash assistance. Uhm, you’ll see in the budget the uhm outyear budget or really ‘26-’28 is flat. Uhm, one piece that admittedly is the changes to mandatory engagement. So, uhm, we are you know working closely with our partners at OMB to try and refine those models uhm, cash assistance though is admittedly more - a more difficult program for us to forecast.
Okay and how much was actually spent on cash assistance in Fiscal 2025?
In ‘25, it was just under $2.7 billion.
And what about to date in Fiscal ‘26?
Through January, we’ve spent $1.6 billion.
Okay. Uhm, as of March, how many cash assistance recipients, individuals and households are there?
Uh, so the overall cash assistance uh case load currently is 585,339 individuals, which is 327,059 cases.
Thank you and how has this number changed over the past several years?

Uhm, I - over the past several years, we’ve seen the cash assistance caseload increase. Uhm, over time, I would say over the last few months we have seen for the first time it actually began to decrease a bit. Uhm, uh, but I think that is a trend that we’re continuing to track to determine if that is actually a trend or some other sort of-
An anomaly perhaps.
An anomaly perhaps.
Because I was going to ask why there’s been such a big increase over the years.

Uh, I think a big increase over the years is really reflective of the need that has been out there in the community. Uhm and you know cash assistance, the eligibility determination is very much based upon income and someone is income eligible or they are not. So, we as an agency continue to do you know that assessment starting in 2023 especially we saw a significant increase in monthly cash assistance uh applications each month and that has really continued. We’ve seen some abating of that but you know we were seeing on average between 45,000 and 50,000 applications for like a multiyear period and many of those people were uh, income eligible for cash assistance. So, they were - were added to the caseload. So, I think it is a - it was a reflection of you know economic realities for uh, low income individuals in New York City and we also made it easier to apply for cash assistance during that period of time. We shifted it to online so individuals did not have to come into one of our sites, which allowed people to also apply whenever it was convenient for them.

Uhm, and I think that also led to an increase in the applications and access to the program.

Uhm, that’s great. That work is great and would love to see more ways that we can make it easier for people to access benefits. Uhm, what services is HRA providing to clients to help them transition from the City FHEPS program to full self sufficiency? And I guess this goes back to your statement Commissioner. Uhm, just you know what effort really are we making to get people out of the program once they’ve been in?

Yeah, no thank you for the question. I think it’s a really important point and effort we should - we should work on together. So, looking at how we can reduce costs of the program. How we can of course move people to self sufficiency. Over that five years, there will be a number of people who we can engage in our career and training programs. We can engage in other subsidy programs to reduce the cost of the program overall. And so, I think there are really some strategies we can use to help people move to self-sufficiency and to limit the cost of the program so that we can serve more people.
Uhm, what have you done already to date? I know, you know you’re talking about things you would like to do in the future, which is all great, but I’m wondering what’s already been done?

Certainly, so to date, you know much of that work would have been focused on individuals who are also on cash assistance and receiving City FHEPS. Uhm, and engaging those individuals in the robust career services programs that we have either through our PACE providers, uhm, as well as other programs such as PINK, Jobs Plus, and our business link program, which offer a variety of different connections to both training, education, as well as we’ve developed a lot of very robust partnerships with employers in the community. Uhm, and connecting people to active employment. So, that’s work that we have been doing that has been really focused on the cash assistance clients uhm, and I think to what the Commissioner is talking about is looking at ways in which we can really expand that to others, people on City FHEPS who could also benefit from those programs.
And what about specifically for City FHEPS, not just Cash Assistance?

Right so, we don’t have a separate specific program for City FHEPS at this time but I think that speaks to some of what the Commissioner was talking about in regards to you know looking forward as well. Uhm, looking at things that can really be targeted at individuals on City FHEPS who may not be connected to other benefits.
Okay.

Right, I think as the Administrator said, there wasn’t a focused effort for City FHEPS only clients. It’s a great opportunity to work with people toward self sufficiency, not waiting till year five. You know starting early, engaging folks and making those pathways out of the program.
Great. Uhm, and do you track how many City FHEPS clients have fully transitioned to self sufficiency?
We can get that number. I know our data, we are tracking City FHEPS quite closely.

That would be great. And we would love to see for Fiscal ‘25 and the Fiscal ‘26 to date, as you’ve been sharing. Thank you.

Uhm, okay, moving to Community Food Connection, CFC funding. Community Food Connection is a vital resource providing much needed food to the city’s vast network of food pantries and soup kitchens. This program is especially important given the current changes to SNAP as a result of the Federal HR1 bill. In the Fiscal 2026 Preliminary Budget response, the Council called on the Administration to increase and baseline the budget to $100 million to help combat the high levels of food insecurity in the city which persists today. I was glad to see that as of the Preliminary Plan, the Fiscal 2026 budget for CFC totals $79.5 million. For the first time in the history of this program, the Preliminary Plan increased the baseline funding by $53.6 million to $74.5 million starting in Fiscal 2027. Is the current Fiscal 2026 budget for CFC an estimate of the need for the whole year or do you expect to add more funding in the Executive plan?
Uhm, no, we believe that this will be the full amount for the budget.
Okay and how will you allocate the additional funding across the CFC network in Fiscal 2027 and the outyears?
Uhm, that’s a good question. We’re still working across our network to work on the distribution plans and our various pantries.

Uhm, while increasing the baseline to 474.5 million is a substantial add. Food insecurity in the city has continued to increase and the inflationary increase in the cost of food puts a burden on the city’s food pantries. Will HRA consider adding annual adjustments to the CFC budget to account for inflation and the increased cost of food procurement?
Uhm, we can talk to our partners at OMB and our partner agencies and explore that yes.
I’ll take that yes at the end there. What is the actual spending thus far in Fiscal 2026 and how much was spent in Fiscal 2025?
Uhm, through January, we’ve spent $37 million. In Fiscal Year ‘25, the program spent $59.1 million.

Thank you. Okay, moving on to HRA staffing levels, uhm, as of January 2026, the

actual headcount for the agency was 10,821 with 1,696 positions vacant or 13.5 percent vacancy rate. What are the main challenges the agency has been experiencing in hiring new candidates?

I mean I think some of it has been similar to what uh, Chief Johns has said before. Uhm, you know in particular when focusing on uh case management and case worker type of positions but I think we have taken a lot of very you know innovative approaches to a., recruiting, uh, nontraditionally as well. So, uh expanding where we are recruiting talent from and where we can you know uh, uh, uh, utilizing incentives, which is we work - we utilize something for the hiring of case workers around that and you know we will continue to sort of focus with our Office of HR solutions to identify additional ways in which we can sort of expand recruitment efforts so that more people know about city opportunities and the pathways that can provide.

Uhm, many of the agency's frontline workers such as eligibility specialists and others involved with the processing of benefit applications and recertifications are in very challenging jobs with low levels of pay. Has the

agency done an evaluation of salary increases for these positions to improve retention and hiring?

Uhm, we’re always looking at retention and hiring and salaries. Uhm, those are conversations that uh we would also have with the City Office of Labor Relations as salaries are baselined within negotiations and agreements with the individual unions that oversee those workers.

Uhm, what is the agency's hiring plan, especially as it relates to frontline client service positions, which I think you got into that a little bit earlier. What are the priority positions the agency is hiring for?

I can speak for HRA. Uhm, I would say for HRA, you know we are always remaining focused on uhm, our benefit opportunity specialists that are in cash assistance, the ES’s who work in SNAP as well as the case workers who work across several of our specialized service programs including APS, HASA uhm and Domestic Violence Services.
And I think frontline workers will always be where we focus our efforts, whether on the DHS side or on the HRA side.
Uhm, what percentage of candidates offered positions accept them?
We’ll have to get back to you on that. We’ll at least get that data from our
Okay, do you have any anecdotal information about the top reasons folks may turn some of these positions down or leave the positions after short periods of time?

I mean, for turnover I will say and acknowledge what you had said, right? Frontline positions in our agency and others uhm, are very challenging right. Uh, we are there to support New Yorkers who may be experiencing a particularly challenging time and so, that is something that we really want to focus on. Uhm, and make sure that we are really providing supports to our staff, right whether it’s through Work Well or other wellness initiatives that really helps to balance and really talk about like self care and what can we bring into these spaces, so that staff can really access those, as well as looking at ways in which we can really show staff that we are invested in them and we want to have them with us for a long time. So, the development of the staff development that I had

talked about before as well, to really especially for frontline staff workers, outline right, what are pathways within the agency that one can really sort of advance uhm within an NC you know across DSS, HRA, DHS that this is a place to create a career, which we have you know, many - you go to many sites and you’ll find people who have worked for our agency for 30, 35 plus years.

And I’ll just add, that’s a great indication of people wanting to continue to work with the agency and we’ll still always create a need for more frontline workers, right. So, even in that scenario, we’re creating - we’re creating that gap. People are moving on to other jobs, that’s a great, that’s a great story and we will always like - there’s just always will be a full court press on frontline staff and creating the pathways I think into those careers, so that people can see their future.

Thank you.Uhm, alright, benefits assistance processing and hiring plan. According to the PMMR, there has been a steady high participation rate in cash assistance and SNAP, with 604,000 individuals receiving cash assistance and

$1.75 million individuals receiving SNAP in the first four months of Fiscal 2026. What is the average monthly volume of new applications and recertifications for each SNAP, Cash Assistance and Medicaid? And would love a comparison to prepandemic levels if possible.

Of course, I do have that. Uhm, so uh the average monthly cash assistance application volume is $46,901 for FY26 to date. Uhm and that is an increase of 77 percent from the same period in FY1, which was an average of $26,494 per month. On SNAP THE average FY26 to date monthly application volume is $29,454 and that is an increase of 14.9 percent from the same period in FY19, which was an average of $25,630. And then for Medicaid, the FY26 year to date application volume is $28,553, which is a 9 percent decrease from the FY19 year to date average of $26,186. I’m sorry, that is an increase, not a decrease.
Oh, thank you.
Yeah.
You said the $28,553 is year to date for FY26.
FY26 and then it’s a 9 percent increase from FY19, which is $26,186.
Okay, got it. Uhm, what percentage of applications and recertifications are denied?

Uhm, I will - I don’t want to speak uh extemporaneously, so I will get back to you on the specific numbers because I know it has transitioned and I think it might be in my book but I don’t know that I underlined that, so we’ll get back to you.
Okay and the reasons for denial would also be helpful.
]Absolutely.
Uhm, and are there bigger delays in each program processing new applications or recertifications?
Uh, no, there are not. We have the extensive delays and backlogs we saw several years ago have been cleared and we have remained - they have remained clear.
Have been fully cleared?

Yeah, the backlogs have been fully cleared and have remained cleared. We obviously

still focus on our timeliness rates right and are always looking to increase those but I will say you know uh, uh, for a majority of like applications that maybe are not uh, done within the 30 day window, they are done shortly afterwards.

Okay, uhm, according to the PMMR, in the first four months of Fiscal 2026, the cash assistance processing timeliness rate was 67 percent and the SNAP processing timeliness rate was 89.9 percent. While these are improvements from the prior year, they’re still below your target of having 95 percent of benefit applications processed within the states required 30 day timeframe. What is the current timeliness rate for cash assistance and SNAP for Fiscal 2026?

Uh, the cumulative rate, I will have to get back to you, though it is remaining consistent with those. I will say on cash assistance, there are some managerial systems, things that we are soon to be implementing that will increase that as well. There’s - I don’t want to get too weedy but there’s -
Get weedy.

There’s different - on cash assistance, there are certain cases called single issuance or one shot deals where uh, the benefit is giving to an individual but there may be a system delay in actually officially closing the case but the timeliness is only calculated on the closingness of the case, so we’re working on making sure that that closing of the case can happen automatically so it will truly reflect that -
Automatically at the time of the one shot deal -
Of issuance of the benefit right?
Okay because my question was going to be, what would cause the discrepancy between the issuance and closing the case?
It may be a staff member delay and going back to officially close the case.
Oh, okay.
And other things, so we’re just looking at instances there.
Sounds like a simple fix.

So, we definitely still you know we still have a ways to go but we’re implementing a variety of you know management and tracking tools to

further increase timeliness to get the 95 percent targets.

Okay and I think that was everything from here. Okay, staff retention rate, going back to this. While the Preliminary Plan has included additional positions for Adult Protective Services, case workers and SNAP eligibility specialists, there’s a growing concern over staff retention and lack of institutional knowledge, which both have a direct impact on agency operations, client service and benefits processing time.
